Tour Diary: Europe '98

The Paternoster

October 14, 1998 // Prague // The Ministry of Culture

The Machine That Never Stops HAZARD

We arrived at the Ministry building for the press junket at 8:00 AM. The promoter had promised "full accessibility." He lied.

The lobby was dominated by a Paternoster—a cyclic elevator with no doors, just a chain of open wooden boxes moving relentlessly upward. Click-clack. Click-clack. You had to hop on while it was moving.

Technical Barrier
  • > The Step: 10-inch lip between floor and car.
  • > The Gap: 4-inch open void to the shaft below.
  • > The Threat: If a caster wheel caught in the gap, the car wouldn't stop. It would crush the chair against the ceiling frame.

Ryan sat in his chair, staring at it. "It's a meat grinder," Evan said, standing protectively between Ryan and the open shaft.

The Urban Legend

The locals joked that if you missed your floor and rode the box "over the top," the gears would grind you to dust. While technically a myth (the car just loops safely over the top), to a man paralyzed from the waist down trapped in a metal frame, the threat felt terrifyingly real.

Ryan famously told the promoter: "I'm not rolling my life into a moving coffin."

The Solution: "Freight Dog" Protocol

There was no other elevator. The interview was on the 6th floor.

Without a word, Tyler Wright handed his backpack to Holly. He grabbed the back handles of Ryan's chair. Evan Wright grabbed the front frame by the knees. They didn't ask for help. They simply tilted Ryan back forty-five degrees and began the climb up six flights of marble stairs.

Ryan did the interview sweating, still covered in the dust of the stairwell. When the journalist asked about his "glamorous rock star life," Ryan just laughed.

The Rider: Clause 12 (Accommodation)

The hardest part of the 1998 tour wasn't the shows; it was the nights.

European hotel rooms were tiny. "Accessible" usually just meant the door was slightly wider. For the O'Connell siblings, this posed a logistical crisis. Privacy had died on I-81 in 1990. Ryan's care—intermittent catheterization, bowel management, skin checks—required assistance that only Cassidy and Holly were trusted to provide.

The "Family Bed" Rule

Holly's tour rider was non-negotiable: "One King Bed. Non-negotiable."

It became an autistic need for both Ryan and Cassidy—the sensory grounding of the "puppy pile." Ryan in the middle (where it was easiest to turn him), Cassidy on his left (her "Safe Side"), Holly on the right (closest to the medical bag). They slept tangled together, a protective knot of limbs that kept the world out and the "Engine" safe.

"We don't need space. We need each other." — Cassidy O'Connell, 1998

The Stardust Engine (ERR-001)

Named after the very first song Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler wrote together at CPI in 1986—celebrating their shared love of the cosmos (“Stardust”) and the rockets to get you there (“Engine”).
